title: Fainting
summary: Fainting or about to faint: lie them down (or sit) before they fall; leg-crossing and muscle tensing if they still feel faint and have no heart attack or stroke signs; get help if it does not improve in 1 to 2 minutes; anyone who actually passed out lies flat (legs raised if uninjured) and needs medical care.

steps.text: Check: do they respond? Are they breathing normally?
steps.detail:
Gasping or occasional breaths are not normal breathing. If you are not sure, treat it as not breathing normally.

Someone who has fainted usually comes round within about a minute (Red Cross).

ask.q: Are they unresponsive and not breathing normally?

steps.text: Breathing but not responding? If they have just gone down, watch their breathing for up to about a minute while they come round. Not breathing normally at any point: start CPR.
steps.detail:
Red Cross: if a person suddenly loses consciousness and then comes to after about a minute, they may simply have fainted. Lie them flat on their back meanwhile.

If at any moment they are not breathing normally (no breathing, or only gasping), do not wait: start CPR now (CPR, adult protocol). If you are not sure, treat it as not breathing normally.

If they never lost consciousness, or are already awake and talking, answer No straight away.

ask.q: After about a minute: are they still not responding?

steps.text: Lie them down on their back where they are, or help them sit down if they cannot lie down. Do this before they fall.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (Class 1): someone who feels faint should take or keep a safe position, such as sitting with help or lying down. The first aim is to stop them falling and getting hurt; about 30% of people admitted to emergency departments after fainting have an injury. Red Cross: have the person lie down on their back. Loosen tight clothing and keep them from getting cold or overheated (Red Cross).

Warning signs of a faint (AHA 2024, Red Cross): lightheadedness or dizziness, pale skin, sweating, changes in vision, weakness, a feeling they are about to faint. Some faints come with no warning at all.

If they hit their head or were hurt in a fall, use the Head injury and concussion protocol as well; if they may have hurt their neck or back, use the Neck or back (spine) injury protocol and do not move them unless you must.

steps.text: Do they have chest pain, trouble breathing, or stroke signs (face drooping, an arm drifting down, slurred speech)?
steps.detail: AHA 2024 (Class 3: Harm): do not use the muscle-tensing manoeuvres in this protocol when signs of a heart attack or stroke come with the faint feeling.

ask.q: Chest pain, trouble breathing, or stroke signs?

steps.text: Did they actually pass out (lose consciousness), even briefly?
Still feeling faint: once they are lying or sitting safely, have them cross their legs and tense the leg muscles hard. Keep it up while the faint feeling lasts.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024: once in a safe position, physical counterpressure manoeuvres (tensing muscles of the legs, arms, belly or neck) can help prevent a faint (Class 2a); leg manoeuvres may be better than arm or belly ones (Class 2b). In trials they roughly halved the risk of fainting. Effects can start within seconds, and continuous manoeuvres helped for at least 2 minutes in tilt-table tests. AHA gives them for faint feelings of vasovagal (reflex) or orthostatic (on standing up) origin.

How: Red Cross: tell the person to cross their legs and/or squeeze their leg muscles. AHA names squatting with the legs crossed as a leg manoeuvre and gripping hard with the hands as an arm one.

Do not use them if there are signs of a heart attack or stroke (AHA 2024, Class 3: Harm).

AHA 2024 (Class 2b): if there is no improvement within 1 to 2 minutes, if they faint, or if symptoms get worse or come back, activate the emergency response system.

ask.q: Within 1 to 2 minutes: are they feeling better?

steps.text: Better: let them get up slowly when ready, sitting first, then standing. Stay beside them in case they feel faint again.
steps.detail: MedlinePlus: get up slowly from lying or sitting. If the faint feeling comes back, lie them down again.

steps.text: Recovered without passing out: let them rest and keep an eye on them for the rest of the day. If the faint feeling comes back or gets worse, or they pass out, get help.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (Class 2b): activate the emergency response system if there is no improvement within 1 to 2 minutes, if they faint, or if symptoms get worse or come back. Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

The Red Cross Fainting page also marks pale skin or sweating, and weakness or dizziness, as needing immediate emergency treatment. This protocol follows AHA 2024 (higher authority, and more specific) for someone who improves within 1 to 2 minutes without passing out; see the open question.

Look for a cause: if they are hot after exertion or in hot weather, use the Heat illness (heat stroke, heat exhaustion, cramps) protocol. If they may be short of fluids (vomiting, diarrhoea, heavy sweating), use the Dehydration protocol. If they have diabetes, check for low blood sugar (Low blood sugar protocol).

steps.text: They passed out: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. Keep them lying flat for at least 10 to 15 minutes; raise the feet if uninjured.
steps.warn: Do not raise the legs if they are injured, or if it causes pain or makes them feel worse.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (6.8, Class 2b): if a faint (syncope) actually occurs, activate the emergency response system. Red Cross Fainting marks loss of consciousness, then coming to in about a minute, as needing immediate emergency treatment. Off-grid, this means getting them to medical care even if they seem fully recovered; the steps below say how urgently. Whether the group wants a narrower rule is an open question for the group; the app follows the guidelines.

Legs: AHA 2024 (section 5.2, Class 2b): with no injury, for example after a simple faint or dehydration, raising the feet about 6 to 12 inches (15 to 30 cm) may be reasonable while waiting for help; if it causes pain or makes them worse, lower them flat again. MedlinePlus: raise the feet about 12 inches (30 cm) above the level of the heart, keep them lying down for at least 10 to 15 minutes, preferably somewhere cool and quiet, and turn them on their side if they vomit. Red Cross does not mention raising the legs.

If they cannot lie down, sit them leaning forward with the head between the knees (MedlinePlus).

Check for injuries from the fall. A blow to the head: use the Head injury and concussion protocol.

Watch their breathing and alertness. If they stop responding and are still breathing, roll them onto their side (Recovery position protocol).

steps.text: Is any of these true: fell from a height or injured, slow to come round, over 50, pregnant, diabetes, chest pain, irregular or pounding heartbeat, fit-like jerking, a bitten tongue, or wet themselves?
steps.detail:
MedlinePlus lists these as reasons to call 911 for a person who fainted: a fall from a height, especially if injured or bleeding; not becoming alert quickly (within a couple of minutes); pregnancy; age over 50; diabetes; chest pain, pressure or discomfort; a pounding or irregular heartbeat; loss of speech, vision problems or being unable to move a limb; convulsions, a tongue injury, or loss of bladder or bowel control.

Chest pain or stroke signs: also use the Chest pain or heart attack protocol, or the Stroke protocol. Diabetes: check for low blood sugar (Low blood sugar protocol).

steps.text: No warning signs: they still need medical care, because they passed out (AHA 2024, Red Cross). Evacuate. Let them get up slowly, never walk alone, and lie down at once if they feel faint again.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (6.8) and Red Cross call for emergency help whenever a faint actually occurs. MedlinePlus: also see a provider for a first-ever faint, frequent faints, or new symptoms with fainting.

Getting up: slowly, sitting first, then standing (MedlinePlus). If the faint feeling comes back, lie them down again at once.

Off-grid (group judgement): with none of the warning signs in the previous step, this is less urgent than those cases, but they still go out to a medical check. They should not walk alone, carry heavy loads, or go near drops or water until checked. Whether the group wants a narrower rule for a typical faint in a young, healthy member is an open question.

Look for a cause: heat (Heat illness (heat stroke, heat exhaustion, cramps) protocol), lack of fluids (Dehydration protocol), diabetes (Low blood sugar protocol).

steps.text: Start CPR now: use the CPR, adult protocol (or CPR, child or CPR, infant).
steps.detail:
Red Cross: if they are unresponsive and not breathing, begin CPR or compression-only CPR and use an AED if one is available.

Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: Not waking: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. If they are not injured, roll them onto their side (Recovery position protocol).
steps.detail:
Red Cross: if they are unresponsive but breathing and not injured, call for help and place them in the recovery position. MedlinePlus: call 911 if they do not become alert within a couple of minutes.

If they may have hurt their head, neck or back in the fall, use the Head injury and concussion protocol or the Neck or back (spine) injury protocol.

Watch their breathing all the time. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR (CPR, adult protocol). Give nothing by mouth.

steps.text: Keep them lying or sitting, whichever is easier for breathing. No muscle-tensing manoeuvres. Use the protocol that fits now (see detail): heart attack, stroke, asthma or allergic reaction.
Get help: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. Keep them lying down and watch their breathing.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024: activate the emergency response system if the faint feeling does not improve within 1 to 2 minutes, if they faint, or if symptoms get worse or come back. MedlinePlus: the warning signs in this protocol (for someone who fainted) need a 911 call.

Keep them lying flat (raise the feet 6 to 12 inches only if they are not injured and it does not make them worse). If they vomit or stop responding but are breathing, roll them onto their side (Recovery position protocol). If they stop breathing normally, start CPR (CPR, adult protocol).

Plan their evacuation: they should not walk out alone, and should lie down at once if the faint feeling returns.

donts: Do not let someone who feels faint stay standing; lie or sit them down first.
Do not use the leg-crossing and muscle-tensing manoeuvres if there are heart attack or stroke signs (AHA 2024: harm).
Do not raise the legs of someone who is injured, or if it hurts or makes them worse (AHA 2024).
Do not let them get up quickly (MedlinePlus).
Do not give anything by mouth until they are fully awake.
evacuate: Get help and evacuate (AHA 2024, Red Cross): anyone who actually passed out, even if they recover; and a faint feeling that does not improve within 1 to 2 minutes, or comes back or gets worse.

Get help urgently (MedlinePlus, for someone who fainted): a fall from a height or injury, not alert within a couple of minutes, pregnancy, over 50, diabetes, chest pain, pounding or irregular heartbeat, speech, vision or limb problems, convulsions, a bitten tongue, or loss of bladder or bowel control.
Medical check (MedlinePlus): a first-ever faint, repeated faints, or new symptoms.
notes: Feeling faint: lie or sit down first, then cross the legs and tense the leg muscles (AHA 2024, Red Cross); not if there are heart attack or stroke signs. Anyone who actually passed out needs medical care (AHA 2024, Red Cross).
